subject: Cache eviction and service headroom design for private GPU pools
messages:
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi@redwood.ai>
To: Ivan Petrov <ivan@edgecloud.io>, Aisha Khan <aisha.k@acme-health.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, Dev Patel <dev@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Cache eviction and service headroom design for private GPU pools

Hi Ivan / Aisha —

Following up from yesterday's call: we sketched a few open questions that will materially change how many GPUs you need in the on-prem pool and the right cache eviction strategy. I attached a first-pass capacity_model_v2.xlsx and the qps_profile_sep.csv you shared. Quick bullets to confirm before we iterate the model:

- Target steady-state throughput: 1,200 concurrent inference requests (chat-style, median 120 tokens generated), goal P50 latency < 140ms per token and P95 < 300ms.
- Cold-KV-cache penalty: when a model warm cache is absent, we measured a ~2.6x increase in GPU time per request on similar workloads — this suggests a deep effect on average tokens/sec across the pool.
- Eviction policy tradeoffs: aggressive eviction (LRU 15m TTL) lowers memory pressure but increases cold-starts, raising tail latency during bursts. Conservative TTL (1h+) reduces cold penalty but requires ~18–22% more GPU headroom to avoid queueing.
- Network egress: you flagged a 6 Gbps per-rack egress constraint — this caps concurrent large-response workloads; included a network_topology_vpc.png for where we think placement and sharding help.

Ask: please confirm the 6 Gbps constraint and whether you can provide per-minute QPS histograms for the last 14 days (we only have the 1-min sampled CSV). With that, we'll finalize a sizing scenario that outputs: GPUs (type & count), expected token/s per-GPU, warm-cache ratio target, and an autoscaling window recommendation.

Thanks,
Naomi
Senior Solutions Architect
Redwood Inference

Attachments: capacity_model_v2.xlsx (spreadsheet), qps_profile_sep.csv (sampled QPS), network_topology_vpc.png (diagram)

Thanks Naomi — quick answers below and a couple clarifications:

- Confirmed: 6 Gbps egress is a hard limit for the current rack (we cannot burst above it without a formal change request).
- We'll upload higher-resolution QPS traces today (5s buckets). Current peak sustained is ~180 RPS for short periods (5–8 min), typical baseline 45–60 RPS. Burst patterns are spiky after product pushes.
- We're open to a hybrid eviction policy — keep hot keys pinned for 20–30 minutes + an LRU for everything else.

One request: can you show a scenario where we keep 3% of requests as cold-starts (i.e., very aggressive pinning for the top 300 prefixes) versus a 12% cold-start scenario? We want the expected impact on required GPUs and on the P95 latency budget.

-Ivan

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi@redwood.ai>, Dev Patel <dev@redwood.ai>

Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 10:22:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Cache eviction and service headroom design for private GPU pools

Adding a technical perspective on GPU accounting and headroom math. Naomi — please feel free to paste this into the model spreadsheet if helpful.

- Baseline perf numbers (on an A100-like 80GB equiv): median tokens/sec (warm) ~ 450, cold ~ 170 (warm/cold ratio ~2.65x). For mixed-precision quantized runs we see warm ~560 and cold ~210. Use conservative warm=420, cold=160 for Acme's latency targets.
- Effective throughput per GPU under load is also a function of batching window. With a 15ms batching window expect ~10–12% throughput uplift vs zero-batch. But batching increases tail latency variance — cap batch window if P95 requirements tight.
- Headroom model: to maintain P95 < 300ms under 95th-percentile arrival rate, provision nominal_capacity = peak_load / utilization_target where utilization_target = 0.65 (allowing room for cache misses + preemption + OS jitter). Example: with 180 RPS peak and average tokens/request=120, tokens/s peak = 21,600. At warm tokens/sec/GPU=420 => need ~52 GPUs nominal. With 12% cold, effective tokens/sec/GPU drops (weighted average) and required GPUs rise to ~59. With 3% cold, requirement is ~53.

I'll add these to sheet 'scenarios' and mark the assumptions cells clearly. Also propose an initial autoscale policy: scale step +3 GPUs, cool-down 180s, scale-out trigger at CPU/GPU util > 70% for 60s, scale-in when util < 45% for 300s (with minimum floor 10 GPUs).

-Marissa
Principal Infrastructure Engineer

Attachment hint: I'll update capacity_model_v2.xlsx with a 'quantized' sheet later.

Subject: Re: Cache eviction and service headroom design for private GPU pools

Appreciate the clarity — a couple of practical constraints from our infra/security teams:

- We cannot persist customer prompts outside the rack for more than 8 hours (retention policy) so long-lived cache pinning beyond that is not allowed.
- We can reserve a small SSD-backed KV store on each node for pinned items (up to 60GB per node) but that means pinned set should be conservative.
- Network team is evaluating request prioritization (marking control-plane calls for lower priority) but that won't be available for 2–3 weeks.

Given the constraints, please produce two final rows in the model: (A) conservative pins (top 100 prefixes pinned, expected cold 9–12%) and (B) aggressive pins (top 300 pinned, expected cold 2–4%) but ensure pinned set fits 60GB/node budget. We want expected GPU counts and a short runbook note on how to detect when pinned-set causes memory pressure.

Thanks,
Aisha
Director, Platform Engineering
Acme Health

Attachments: none

Thanks all — final deliverables we will push by EOD tomorrow:

1) capacity_model_v2.xlsx updated with rows for 'conservative pins (100)', 'balanced (200)', and 'aggressive (300)'. Each row will include: assumed warm/cold ratio, tokens/sec per-GPU, GPU count (min/nominal/peak), network egress estimate per-rack, and pinned-set size.
2) A short runbook (1 page) with detection signals: KV eviction rate > 5%/min, GPU queue depth > 80 for 60s, P95 latency drift > 20% over baseline — and actions (increase pinned TTL, add +2 GPUs, throttle large responses).
3) A proposed autoscale config (Marissa's draft) and a note on batch-window tradeoffs that ops can toggle live.

Dev / Sean — please coordinate on the runbook steps and let me know if the detection thresholds need adjusting (Sean: you own the alerting playbook). Ivan / Aisha — once you confirm the 5s QPS traces are uploaded, we'll produce the final numeric table.

Best,
Naomi
Senior Solutions Architect
Redwood Inference

Attachments to follow: capacity_model_v2.xlsx (updated), short_runbook_cache_headroom.md
